intro: In September 1955 a Chicago mother opened her murdered son's casket and made the country look. In November 2008 a crowd of more than two hundred thousand stood in Grant Park to watch a senator from Illinois become president. Between those two nights lie the years this unit covers: the civil rights movement and the movements it inspired, the collapse of trust after Vietnam and Watergate, the oil shocks, the conservative turn, the end of the Cold War, the internet, September 11, the crash of 2008, a decade of polarization and a pandemic. Much of it happened on the streets and in the courtrooms of Chicago, and some of it happened to your own family.

This is the hardest history in the course, for two reasons. The first is that it is not finished: the arguments about what these events meant are still going on, and the people making them are still alive. The second is that the evidence is strange. Some of it is on tape in the National Archives; some of it is a deleted post or a text on a phone that no longer turns on. To study this era you have to learn what historians do when the records are incomplete, the outcomes unknown and the writer is also a witness.

By the end of the unit you should be able to explain how a movement with no army forced a nation to change its laws, how each shock since 1969 changed what Americans expected from their government, and how to weigh a claim about the recent past against the evidence that exists now and the evidence still to come. You should also be able to say, with reasons, which of these events changed the country and which only seemed to at the time.
bigQuestion: From the civil rights movement to the present, which events actually changed the United States, and how can we judge a past whose evidence is still arriving and whose witnesses are still arguing?

timeline.t: Brown v. Board of Education rules that segregated public schools are unconstitutional
Emmett Till's open-casket funeral in Chicago; the Montgomery bus boycott begins in December
Birmingham, the March on Washington and the church bombing that killed four girls
Congress passes the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act
Martin Luther King Jr. moves to Chicago's West Side to fight housing segregation
The Supreme Court orders the tapes released; Nixon resigns on August 9
Ronald Reagan of Tampico and Dixon, Illinois, wins the presidency; Wisconsin Steel closes
The Berlin Wall opens on November 9; the Soviet Union dissolves two years later
Mosaic, the first popular web browser, is released at the University of Illinois
Al-Qaeda attacks kill nearly three thousand on September 11; the war in Afghanistan begins
Lehman Brothers collapses in September; Barack Obama is elected in November
The COVID-19 pandemic closes schools and workplaces; protests follow the killing of George Floyd

words.d: the 1954 Supreme Court decision that separate schools are inherently unequal
protest that confronts an injustice in person, such as sit-ins, boycotts and marches
the 1965 law that banned literacy tests and sent federal registrars to the South
the late-1960s call for Black self-determination, pride and control of Black communities
the 1972 break-in and cover-up that forced President Nixon to resign in 1974
high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, as in the 1970s
the theory that tax cuts will spur enough growth to raise revenue, tried under Reagan
Gorbachev's policy of openness in the Soviet Union after 1985
the tightening links of trade, money, people and information across borders
the October 2001 law that expanded government surveillance powers after September 11
the downturn from December 2007 to June 2009 caused by the housing and financial collapse
the movement of the two parties and their supporters toward opposite poles with little overlap

test.q: Why did Mamie Till-Mobley insist on an open casket in 1955?
choices: So the world would see what had been done to her son, turning private grief into public evidence
Because Mississippi law required it
Because the funeral home refused to close it
Because the trial had already ended
test.why: She said she wanted the world to see; the photograph in Jet moved a generation into the movement.

test.q: What was the relationship between Brown v. Board and the direct action that followed?
choices: Brown ended segregation, so no protest was needed
Brown gave the movement a legal foundation, but protest and later laws were needed to enforce it
Brown applied only to buses
Brown was reversed by the sit-ins
test.why: The 1954 ruling was not enforced until people and the 1964 and 1965 acts forced the issue.

test.q: What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 do that earlier laws had not?
choices: It gave women the vote
It desegregated lunch counters
It banned literacy tests and sent federal officials to register voters in resistant counties
It lowered the voting age to eighteen
test.why: Federal enforcement, not just a promise, is what raised Black registration in the Deep South within a few years.

test.q: What did King find in Chicago in 1966 that differed from the South?
choices: No segregation at all
Laws requiring segregated schools
Full support from city hall
Segregation enforced by housing markets, real estate practices and neighborhood violence rather than by law
test.why: Chicago had no Jim Crow statutes, but housing patterns and mob resistance produced a different kind of wall.

test.q: Which was a strategy shared by the women's, disability and LGBTQ rights movements that followed the civil rights movement?
choices: Using courts, protest and legislation together to change law and public opinion
Forming their own armies
Refusing to work with lawyers
Seeking to leave the United States
test.why: Later movements adopted the civil rights toolkit of lawsuits, direct action and lobbying.

test.q: What did the tape of June 23, 1972, prove?
choices: That Nixon had ordered the burglars to break in
That Nixon had told aides to have the CIA block the FBI's investigation, an obstruction of justice
That Nixon had won the election fairly
That Congress had bugged the White House
test.why: The so-called smoking gun tape ended Republican support in the Senate and led to his resignation.

test.q: How did Congress respond to the abuses revealed in the 1970s?
choices: It expanded the president's war powers
It abolished the FBI
It passed the War Powers Resolution, strengthened FOIA and created intelligence oversight committees
It repealed the Twenty-sixth Amendment
test.why: These laws limited presidents and opened records after Vietnam, Watergate and the Church Committee.

test.q: What ended the inflation of the 1970s?
choices: The 1973 oil embargo
Wage and price freezes
NAFTA
Very high interest rates set by the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker, at the cost of a deep recession
test.why: Rates above twenty percent brought inflation to about three percent by 1983 while unemployment neared eleven percent.

test.q: Which Illinois connection to the conservative movement does the unit describe?
choices: Reagan's birth in Tampico and Phyllis Schlafly's campaign from Alton against the Equal Rights Amendment
The founding of the Republican Party in Chicago
Illinois ratifying the Equal Rights Amendment first
Reagan's governorship of Illinois
test.why: Reagan grew up in Dixon; Schlafly's STOP ERA made Illinois the key battleground.

test.q: Which explanation for the end of the Cold War would Soviet archives be most likely to test?
choices: That the Berlin Wall was tall
That Gorbachev chose not to send tanks and that the economy could not sustain the arms race
That Mosaic spread information
That NAFTA weakened the Soviet Union
test.why: Soviet records reveal what its leaders thought they could afford and why they held back force.

test.q: What did the University of Illinois contribute to the 1990s?
choices: The first internet network
The World Wide Web
Mosaic, the first popular web browser, released in 1993
The first online bank
test.why: Mosaic from the National Center for Supercomputing Applications made the web usable for ordinary people.

test.q: How did trust in government move after September 11, 2001?
choices: It fell to its lowest level ever
It stayed exactly the same
It disappeared
It spiked to levels not seen since the 1960s, then fell back to about one in five within a decade
test.why: Polling shows a brief jump to about sixty percent in late 2001, followed by a long decline.

test.q: What made the 2008 financial crisis spread beyond mortgage borrowers?
choices: Mortgages had been bundled into bonds sold worldwide and rated safe, so falling home prices caused losses everywhere
Every American owned a second home
The government had banned foreclosures
Banks had stopped lending in 2005
test.why: Securitization tied global banks and insurers to subprime loans.

test.q: What pattern links the Obama health law of 2010 and the Republican midterm win that year?
choices: Both were unanimous
A major law passed on party lines, and the president's party then lost heavily in the midterm, a sign of polarization
Both were decided by the Supreme Court
Both happened before the 2008 election
test.why: Every Republican opposed the Affordable Care Act, and Democrats lost sixty-three House seats months later.

test.q: Which method does the unit recommend for judging events you lived through?
choices: Trust your memory alone
Wait until every witness has died
Source and corroborate claims, watch for hindsight and presentism, and save records for future historians
Read only the most shared posts
test.why: The final chapter sets out the rules historians use when the writer is also a witness.

write.prompt: Choose one event from this unit after 1968 and make a claim: did it change the United States as much as people believed at the time, more, or less? Support your claim with at least three pieces of evidence from the unit, including one number or document, and explain what evidence from the future could change your answer.
tips: State your claim in one sentence that names the event and takes a clear position on how much it changed.
Use specific evidence: a poll number, a law, an unemployment rate, a court ruling, a document, with its date.
Explain your reasoning: why does each piece of evidence show change or the lack of it?
Give the other side its best argument, then say why your evidence outweighs it.
End by naming one record, not yet open or not yet saved, that could change how historians judge this event.
